38.0.0.en: 1 Honour a physician with the honour due unto him for the uses which ye may have of him: for the Lord hath created him. 2 For of the most High cometh healing, and he shall receive honour of the king. 3 The skill of the physician shall lift up his head: and in the sight of great men he shall be in admiration. 4 The Lord hath created medicines out of the earth; and he that is wise will not abhor them. 5 Was not the water made sweet with wood, that the virtue thereof might be known? 6 And he hath given men skill, that he might be honoured in his marvellous works. 7 With such doth he heal [men], and taketh away their pains. Of such doth the apothecary make a confection; and of his works there is no end. 8 And from him is peace over all the earth. 9 My son, in thy sickness be not negligent: but pray unto the Lord, and he will make thee whole. 10 Leave off from sin, and order thine hands aright, and cleanse thy heart from all wickedness. 11 Give a sweet savour, and a memorial of fine flour; and make a fat offering, as not being. 12 Then give place to the physician, for the Lord hath created him: let him not go from thee, for thou hast need of him. 13 There is a time when in their hands there is good success. 14 For they shall also pray unto the Lord, that he would prosper that which they give for ease and remedy to prolong life. 15 He that sinneth before his Maker, let him fall into the hand of the physician.

38.0.1.en: The subject of medicine is bound up with wisdom, for the physician is committed to studying medicine and drugs, and wisdom is granted to him from God to practise his work; therefore the physician is still called among the common people "the wise man" (hakim). Among the Rabbis, and those who were later known as the Hasidim, that is, the pious, it prevailed that resorting to the physician is a weakness of faith in God, relying on what is recorded in (2 Chr 16:12) that King Asa sought the physicians and not the Lord. These physicians often used magic and divination, and did not turn to God while using the art of medicine. Ben Sira was sympathetic to progress in the field of medicine and drugs, so he spoke of the importance of the physician and his esteem for medicine.

38.0.2.en: St. Basil the Great, together with his friend St. Gregory of Nazianzus, realized their mission while they were students at the University of Athens, forming a group among the students that had its esteem and respect even among the philosophers, the university professors. This drove him to make prominent that he saw medicine as a gift and endowment from God like all other gifts and arts, so that it is not permissible to resist or ignore it, but to care for the study of this art or craft with esteem and respect for it.

38.0.3.en: As for the physician, God created him to work according to his gift and study, yet the true healer is God. The physician offers the blessing of health as a gift from God, and this calls us to honor the physician. And medicine is one of the divine gifts offered to men, like the sun and the rain, which are given to sinners as to the righteous, as the Lord Christ said.

38.0.4.en: v Question: Is resorting to the art of medicine consistent with the practice of godliness?

38.0.5.en: Answer: Every art is a gift of God, to remedy the defect in nature. An example of this is the art of agriculture, to remedy the produce of the earth when the produce is not sufficient to satisfy our needs. And the art of weaving, to make the clothing necessary for modesty and for protection from the winds. In the same way the art of building. The same is true of the art of medicine; since our body is exposed to various kinds of harm, some attacking from outside, and some from inside because of the food we take, and since the body suffers because of excess of eating or lack of it, the art of medicine was given by God to guide our whole life, as an example of the healing of the soul, leading us to remove what is excessive and to add what is lacking...

38.0.6.en: When we were commanded to return to the dust from which we were taken, and we came to have a body ridden by pain, whose destiny became destruction because of sin, and for the same reason it was also subjected to sickness, we have the art of medicine to help the sick at least to some extent[1].

38.0.7.en: St. Basil the Great Give to the physician the honor that is fitting for him, and also according to your need of him, for the Lord created him [1].

38.1.0.en: By the incarnation of the Word the Creator confirmed His honoring of the body, and in His ministry He healed many so that no one might think that He rejects the body, but rather seeks its wholeness, as He grants it eternal glory together with the soul. And by His saying: "They that are whole need not a physician, but they that are sick: I came not to call the righteous, but sinners to repentance" (Mk 12:17), He did not disdain to call Himself a physician. St. Justin sees in the Lord Christ's saying an open door for the body, which some heresies attacked as being a sinner unworthy of resurrection with the soul, for he said: [If the flesh is the sinner, the Savior came for the sake of sinners, for He says: "I came not to call the righteous, but sinners to repentance." By this He shows the flesh its value in the eyes of God, and that it is glorified... and it must be saved[2].]

38.1.1.en: For healing comes from the Most High, and from the king (the physician) receives gifts [2].

38.1.2.en: God gives the physician understanding and wisdom, and it is He who offers us healing through the physician. If the king honors the successful physician and gives him gifts, it befits the king as well as the physician to thank God, the giver of healing.

38.2.0.en: v O brother, some people resort to physicians, and others do not go to them. Those who resort to them do so with their hope in God, saying: "In the name of the Lord we entrust ourselves to the physicians, for He grants healing through them." And those who do not resort to them do not do so, and they have hope in the name of God, and He heals them. So if you resort to physicians you do not commit a fault, and those who do not resort to them are not proud[3].

38.3.0.en: v A person must remember that without God not even the physician can do anything. Rather it is God who grants healing to the sick when He wills it[4].

38.3.1.en: St. Barsanuphius The skill of the physician lifts up his head, and he is admired in the presence of great men [3].

38.4.0.en: In speaking of the success of his ministry and the ministry of Apollos in Corinth, the Apostle Paul says: "I have planted, Apollos watered; but God gave the increase" (1 Cor 3:6). So it is with physicians: they provide the medicine, and God is the one who heals. St. Augustine says: [What is the use if we plant or water if God does not give the increase? For neither is he that planteth any thing, neither he that watereth, but God that giveth the increase[5].] By the same logic we say: [What is the use if the physician treats the patient if God does not heal?]

38.4.1.en: The Lord created medicines out of the earth, and the wise man will not despise them [4].

38.4.2.en: St. Macarius the Great sees in the making of medicines God's wonderful care for man. For if diseases came upon man because of his neglect of the heavenly and his preoccupation with earthly things, God gave the earth so that it might provide medicines from the herbs that grow from the earth.

38.5.0.en: v God gave the earth and its drugs for the healing of the body, issuing a command that the body that is of dust be treated with things taken from the dust (herbs)... After man fell from Paradise he came at once under the influence of the sicknesses and disturbances of the body... Therefore God gave the world medicine for its relief, for the healing and care of the body, and permitted those who cannot entrust themselves wholly into the hands of God to use it[6].

38.5.1.en: St. Macarius the Great v Sometimes God sees that it is better to heal us secretly without visible means [such as resorting to a physician and using a medicine] when He sees that this means is useful for our souls. At other times He wants us to use medicines for the treatment of our illnesses, either so as to imprint on our souls the remembrance of His grace which we receive through our slow healing, or, as I said, to offer us an example to imitate concerning care for the soul. For just as in the case of the body it is necessary to get rid of the elements foreign to it and to add to it what is lacking, so in the case of the soul it befits us to get rid of what is foreign to it, and to accept what is in harmony with its nature. For God made man upright (Eccl 7:29) and created us for good works that we should walk in them (Eph 10:2).

38.6.0.en: St. Basil the Great Was not the water made sweet with wood[7], that the virtue thereof might be known? [5]

38.6.1.en: Here he refers to what is recorded in (Ex 15:24), when the people felt thirst and murmured against Moses, for they found bitter water that could not quench their thirst. Moses the prophet cast the tree into the bitter waters and they became sweet. Thus the power of God was known through the tree that was cast into the bitter spring, so that its waters became sweet.

38.7.0.en: Many of the Fathers see in the tree a type of the Cross that works in the waters of Baptism, so that our life is changed from bitterness to sweetness, and instead of bearing the works of the old man we enjoy the new nature that has become ours in Christ Jesus[8]. St. Ambrose says: [Marah was a spring of intense bitterness, but when Moses cast the tree into it, it became sweet water. For water without the preaching of the Lord's Cross is of no benefit for the coming salvation. But after it has been consecrated by the mystery of the saving Cross it becomes fit for use in the spiritual font and the cup of salvation; for just as Moses the prophet cast the wood into that spring, so too the priest pronounces over the baptismal font the testimony of the Lord's Cross, and the water becomes sweet because of the work of grace[9].]

38.7.1.en: And it is He (the Lord) who gave men skill, that He might be glorified in His wonders [6].

38.7.2.en: What is the wonder in His giving men skill? He honors man, giving him reason and understanding and the ability to work, while God Himself is the giver of healing through the work of the physician.

38.7.3.en: With medicines He heals, and takes away pains, and of them the pharmacist makes mixtures [7].

38.7.4.en: Ben Sira is careful to affirm the need for human work to be in harmony with divine work and sanctified by it, and for our will to be joined to the divine will and sanctified. The physician has his role in obtaining healing and his skill is a gift from God, the medicine is extracted from herbs and plants, and the pharmacist prepares and mixes it.

38.7.5.en: And the works of God have no end, and through Him health comes upon the face of the earth [8].

38.8.0.en: My son, when you are sick do not be negligent, but pray to the Lord, and He will heal you [9].

38.8.1.en: With the affirmation of God's work and our dependence on Him, it is fitting that we not neglect our bodily health, but ask God for healing. Moreover, our being struck by any illness gives us first the opportunity to review our spiritual accounts, confessing our sins, giving thanks to God, and praying so as to enjoy the work of God in us.

38.9.0.en: v Sickness of the body restrains sin, and luxury kindles the fire of the sin of the flesh[10].

38.9.1.en: v When we suffer the blows of trials from the hand of God, who directs our life with goodness and wisdom, we must first ask Him to grant us to understand the reason for our being afflicted with these blows, and second ask Him for our deliverance from our sufferings or that He give us patience to bear them to the end, for God gives us with the temptation the way out to bear it (1 Cor 13:10).

38.9.2.en: St. Basil the Great Leave off your iniquities, and make your hands upright, and cleanse your heart from all sin [10].

38.9.3.en: The believer seizes every opportunity, among them sickness, for a new start in the spiritual life and for the enjoyment of purity of heart.

38.9.4.en: v We must also give proof of the reform of ourselves by bringing forth fruits worthy of repentance (Lk 8:3), remembering the words of the Lord: "Behold, thou art made whole: sin no more, lest a worse thing come unto thee" (Jn 14:5).

38.10.0.en: St. Basil the Great Offer a sacrifice of sweet savour, and a memorial of fine flour, and pour oil upon your offering, as though you were to die soon [11].

38.10.1.en: The offering of the sacrifice of love, thanksgiving and praise does not leave our hearts even in the moments of death, for it is a preparation for our departure from this world.

38.10.2.en: v When we receive healing from God... we must receive this with thanksgiving. Let us behold God's care watching over us without distinction, whether the healing takes place through an unseen source or through a material thing (medicine), and let us accept the latter healing as a gift from the hand of God.

38.10.3.en: v Lazarus, in spite of suffering painful sores, never murmured against the rich man, nor asked him for anything, and therefore found rest in the bosom of Abraham, as one who humbly accepted the trials of life (including his sickness)[11].

38.11.0.en: St. Basil the Great Keep in touch with your physician, for the Lord created him, and do not let him leave you, for you need him [12].

38.12.0.en: There is a time when success is in their hands [13].

38.13.0.en: For they too pray to the Lord that their work may succeed in bringing relief and healing, for the preservation of your life [14].

38.13.1.en: Our faith in God, the Physician of our souls and our bodies, does not call us to neglect our health or not to resort to medicine and drugs. Moreover, it befits the physician to turn to God that He may give him wisdom and blessing in his work.

38.14.0.en: He who sins before his Maker may fall into the hands of a physician [15].

38.14.1.en: The Lord permits bodily sickness so that we may care for the sicknesses of the spirit, which we so often disregard.

38.14.2.en: v When we are granted the blessing of healing, whether by means of wine mixed with oil, as in the case of the man who fell among thieves (Lk 10:34), or by means of a fig, as in the case of Hezekiah, we receive it with thanksgiving. Besides that, we look to God's care watching over us without partiality, whether it is accomplished through an unseen source or a material agency; for in the latter a more vivid awareness is truly born in us of the kindness that comes from the hands of God.

38.14.3.en: Often the sicknesses that befall us come for our benefit, and our submission to painful treatment is part of the ordering of our life. Therefore sound prudence dictates to us not to protest against amputation or cauterizing, or against bearing the bitterness of an unwelcome medicine, or abstaining from food, or following a diet, and being committed to abstaining from harmful things. We must also keep to our goal, namely our spiritual benefit, as the care of the soul teaches us by analogy (with the care of the body)[12].

38.15.s.en: 2. Mourning for the dead for a time

38.15.0.en: 16 My son, shed tears over the dead, and begin lamentation as befits one who has suffered a great calamity, and shroud his body as is right, and do not neglect his burial. 17 Let your weeping be bitter, and burn in wailing. 18 Hold the mourning according to his rank, a day or two, to avoid slander, then be comforted for your grief. 19 For grief brings death, and heaviness of heart bends strength. 20 In solitude grief grows strong, and the life of the wretched is according to his heart. 21 Do not give your heart over to grief, but drive it away, remembering the last things. 22 Do not forget, for there is no return from there, and you do not profit him, but you harm yourself. 23 Remember that what was decreed for him is decreed for you. Yesterday for me and today for you. 24 When the dead is at rest, rest from remembering him, and be comforted for him when his spirit departs. 1. The Jews surpassed many peoples in their treatment of the dead, such as the Romans and the Etruscons. In Italy, when the Romans gained control over the Etruscons, the latter burned the bodies of their dead and the Romans burned them until they became ashes. In the Bible, in both its Testaments, we hear only of the burial of the dead, and the believers held to the resurrection of the bodies as it came in (2 Kgs 7). The New Testament affirmed this (Heb 11:35; Acts 2:32, 36; 13:31-32; 24:13-15). With the spread of the faith in Hellenistic/Roman culture, the culture adopted the idea of burial instead of the burning of corpses. In Rome there were the burial places in underground catacombs before the building of churches. 2. The Law allowed the burning of the bodies of the dead in two cases: the one who dies under a curse, as in the case of Achan the son of Carmi and his family, who were burned after being stoned (Josh 25:7); and the guilty one who is caught in the sin of adultery (Lev 20:14; 21:9). 3. In general, the Jews were careful to wash their dead as quickly as possible, then to bury them in a ceremony marked by simplicity after a prayer or the hymns of the Kaddish was recited, which is an Aramaic word meaning holy. There are at present four basic kinds of Kaddish. And when the Kaddish is recited as a prayer of mourning for the souls of the dead, the son of the dead man does the recitation, and if there is no son, a mature male of the family, or any volunteer Jew. The chanting of the Kaddish continues for eleven months and one day from the date of death. The reason for the length of this period is the Jews' belief that the punishment of the wicked in Gehenna lasts a whole year, and so the recitation of the Kaddish must stop before the completion of the year so that it may not appear that the deceased was among the guilty; the Kaddish is also recited on the anniversary. 4. Because of the climate, burial usually took place immediately after death, and because they did not embalm the dead like the Egyptians, nor burn them like the Romans. They used embalming for Jacob and Joseph, who died in Egypt, and they were placed in coffins. 5. Jewish cemeteries are called "the house of the living" or "the house of eternity." They regarded the place where a Jew is buried as holy. Perhaps this excessive concern for the body of the dead explains Israel's concern to recover the bodies of the slain. 6. Professional mourning women: the family and friends carry out the lamenting and weeping for the dead, led in this by a professional "mourning woman," so that their clamor and wailing rise resounding and echoing (Eccl 12:5; Amos 5:16). 7. Excessive grief: sometimes excessive grief leads some extremists to inflict wounds on their bodies. The Law forbade the people of Israel from such an act (Lev 19:28; 21:5; 2 Sam 1:11-12; Lam 1:16). 8. The body that is not buried in the earth is considered a shame for the family and brings a curse on the land, so even the bodies of criminals must be buried (Deut 21:22-23). 9. The Jews visit the graves on feast days to offer prayers before the tombs of the dead so that they may intercede for them with God.

38.15.1.en: My son, shed tears over the dead, and begin to lament as befits one upon whom a grave calamity has come.

38.15.2.en: Shroud his body with honor as is due to him, and take care of his burial [16].

38.16.0.en: When Lazarus died it was said: "Jesus wept" (Jn 11:35). Ben Sira did not ignore the feelings of separation, but he encouraged a quick return to normal life, because the dead man does not benefit from the tears of those who grieve over him. And excessive grief is harmful to body and soul [19-23].

38.16.1.en: v The Lord wept for Lazarus, whom He was about to raise to life, doubtless in order to allow us by His example to weep for our dead, even though He did not give us His commandment to that effect, this with our faith that they rise to the true life. It was not at random that it was said: "Shed tears over the dead, and begin to lament as one who has suffered great harm," but he goes on a little later to say: "and be comforted for thy heaviness, for of heaviness cometh death, and the heaviness of the heart breaketh strength"[13].

38.16.2.en: St. Augustine v In order that the Savior Himself might show that He has real human feelings, He grieved for the one whom He was about to raise from the dead[14].

38.16.3.en: St. Jerome Weep bitterly, and lament with warmth, and hold the mourning according to his rank a day or two, to avoid slander, then be comforted for your sorrow [17].

38.16.4.en: Bitter weeping here means weeping with sincere feelings, and not for outward show for the sake of those taking part in the funeral service. This sincerity is better than lamentation, for many lament the dead man and praise him not from the heart.

38.16.5.en: Ben Sira did not forbid mourning for the dead, but within the limit of two days to bring out sincere feelings. After that the person declares his practical consolation by returning to his work and his obligations, taking warning from death as a passage into Paradise.

38.16.6.en: v Guard against surrounding yourself with the tyrant of grief. You can control yourself, for the storm is not greater than your skill.

38.16.7.en: v Never be depressed, for there is only one thing to be feared, and that is sin.

38.16.8.en: v Do not look at the body lying with closed eyes and silent lips, but at the man who has risen and is enjoying the unspeakable and wonderful glory; direct your thoughts from the present sight to the coming hope[15].

38.16.9.en: v Have you been deprived of meeting him, so that you weep and grieve? Now is this not something unreasonable? If you gave your daughter in marriage and her husband took her to a far country where she enjoys wealth there, you do not count this a catastrophe, but their riches console you for the grief caused by her absence. And now here it is not a man but the Lord Himself who takes your relative, so do you grieve and lament?[16]

38.16.10.en: v You may grieve and weep, but do not let despair come upon you, and do not be absorbed in complaints. Thank God who took your friend, so that you may find an opportunity to honor the departed, and his separation from you becomes a mourning. If you fall into a state of dejection, you withhold honor from the departed, and grieve God who took him, and harm yourself. But if you are thankful you honor the departed and glorify God and you yourself benefit. Weep as your Lord wept for Lazarus, observing the proper limits of grief, which you must not transgress. So also Paul says: "I would not have you to be ignorant, brethren, concerning them which are asleep, that ye sorrow not, even as others which have no hope" (1 Thess 4:13). He says: "Do not grieve like the Greeks, who have no hope of the resurrection, who despair of the life to come[17].

38.16.11.en: St. John Chrysostom For of heaviness cometh death, and the heaviness of the heart breaketh your strength [18].

38.16.12.en: There are two kinds of grief: holy grief, which is mingled with a spirit of hope, like Peter's grief after his fall; and extreme grief without hope, like the grief of Judas, which drove him to suicide. Excess of grief brings dejection, despair and weariness, takes away a man's vitality and breaks his heart, and he is counted dead.

38.16.13.en: v Excessive grief is a dreadful thing that begets death. Therefore Paul says: "lest perhaps such a one should be swallowed up with overmuch sorrow" (2 Cor 2:7)[18].

38.16.14.en: v Satan can destroy even under the appearance of godliness. For he is able to destroy not only by leading a person to fornication but sometimes, on the contrary, by excessive grief that makes despair follow repentance. To snare us by sin is his proper work, but to snare us in our repentance is a refined disgrace, for he fights us with our weapon and not with his own[19].

38.16.15.en: St. John Chrysostom Also, in affliction sorrow remaineth, and the life of the poor is the heaviness of his heart [19].

38.17.0.en: Do not give your heart over to grief, but drive it away, remembering the end of life [20].

38.17.1.en: v For your sake, O man, He prepared the Kingdom! And for your sake He prepared unspeakable good things, and a portion made ready in heaven, and a life without parallel, and a joy that cannot be uttered!

38.18.0.en: St. John Chrysostom Do not forget that there is no return (from there), and you will not profit the dead by grief, but only hurt yourself [21].

38.18.1.en: St. John Chrysostom presents to us a view of faith that challenges death, through which, instead of excessive grief over the dead, we count him blessed because he has departed to enjoy what surpasses nature.

38.18.2.en: v In his preaching (the Apostle Paul) grew in honor by accepting insults and persecutions, looking at death as we look at life, accepting poverty as we accept wealth, enjoying labors as we seek rest, preferring affliction to pleasure, and praying for his enemies more than those who pray against them. So he overturned the order of things, or rather let us say that it is we who changed those systems. For he simply kept the laws of God, because what he sought agrees with human nature, while what we seek is against nature[20].

38.18.3.en: St. John Chrysostom Remember my end, for your end will be like it:

38.19.0.en: "Yesterday for me, and today for you" [22].

38.19.1.en: v Look at me, my companions who accompany me and bury me, and let not the temporal dwelling lead you astray as it led me astray.

38.19.2.en: Flee from the world, flee from wealth and from iniquity; come and see how the way out of the road has been crossed.

38.19.3.en: Look at me, my friends, how I ran, and how I became rich, and here I go out stripped of my possessions.

38.19.4.en: You accompanied me, so remember your own selves because of me; the road is common, so make smooth, make smooth your paths.

38.19.5.en: The dead man says these things to all his relatives by his silence, and the sight of him is of benefit to the discerning.

38.19.6.en: Whoever does not profit from teaching by words, let him look at nature (and see) what his end is, and repent.

38.19.7.en: If the hearer denies the written Law, lifeless nature casts terror upon those who look.

38.19.8.en: The end of the dead man becomes a good cause for the living, that each one may remember himself and return to repentance.

38.19.9.en: Behold teaching without discourses or words; blessed is he who by his death despised the world lest he covet[21].

38.20.0.en: St. Mar Jacob of Serugh When the dead man is at rest, let his remembrance rest, and be comforted for him when his spirit departs [23].

38.20.1.en: The talk of the rest of the dead man comes from Ben Sira's faith in life after death.

38.21.0.en: 25 The scribe acquires wisdom in the time of leisure, and he who has little business obtains it. 26 How shall he get wisdom who holds the plough, and glories in the goad, and drives the oxen, and is occupied in their works, and whose talk is of the young of bulls? 27 His heart is on the furrows of the plough, and his watching is in fattening the heifers. 28 So also every craftsman and engineer who spends the night as the day, and those who engrave the signets of seals, who strive in varying the shapes, whose hearts are set on representing the image like its original, and whose watching is in completing their craft. 29 So also the smith sitting by the anvil, bent over forging a massive piece of iron; the blaze of the fire hardens his flesh, and he struggles with the heat of the furnace. 30 The sound of the hammer is continually in his ears, and his eyes are on the pattern of the thing made. 31 His heart is set on completing the works, and his watching is in adorning them to perfection. 32 And so the potter sitting at his work, turning his wheel with his feet; he is ever anxious about his work, and counts all his products. 33 With his arm he kneads the clay, and before his feet he bends its strength. 34 His heart is set on perfecting the glaze, and his watching is in cleaning the furnace. 35 All these rely on their hands, and each of them is wise in his craft. 36 Without them a city is not built. 37 They do not dwell in cities, nor walk about, nor enter the assembly, 38 nor sit on the judge's seat, nor understand the arts of lawsuits, nor expound judgment and justice, nor utter proverbs. 39 But they keep the things of the age in order, and their prayer is for the work of their craft, unlike the one who gives himself to meditation on the law of the Most High.

38.21.1.en: With the role of leaders, among them the scribes, in the progress of society, Ben Sira honors the craftsmen and those with manual skills, because society depends on them for progress and prosperity. He speaks of craftsmen and those who work in animal husbandry [25-26], carpenters and sculptors [27], metalworkers [28] and potters [29-30]. These provide the materials that the leaders and scribes use. Ben Sira did not belittle any work in society.

38.21.2.en: If the Jews exempt the Rabbis from some works and crafts, it is not out of contempt for these works, but so that they may devote themselves to pastoral care, service and worship. But often every Jew, whatever his position, learns a manual trade that he practises when necessary. This is clear in the life of Saul of Tarsus the Pharisee, and also Aquila and Priscilla; they were all tentmakers (1 Cor 9:4-11). And in the monastic system manual work is obligatory for all, even if they are heads of monasteries or do intellectual work such as teaching.

38.21.3.en: The wisdom of the scribe depends on his opportunity for solitude, and when he has little work he becomes wise [24].

38.21.4.en: v "I sleep, but my heart waketh." I rest from being occupied with activities, but my mind directs all its energies toward the inclination of clinging to God[22].

38.21.5.en: St. Augustine How shall he become wise who holds the plough? For he glories in the shaft of the goad, and drives the ox, and is occupied with the laborers, and his talk is of the young of animals [25]

38.21.6.en: The goad is the rod with which we prick some animals; the shepherd uses it in leading sheep and animals.

38.22.0.en: His heart is turned to the furrows of the plough, and his watching is in fattening the calves [26].

38.22.1.en: It is good that the farmer be faithful in his work, but he can enjoy wisdom, which is the adornment of life and without which life is not possible. His work confines him to a narrow material circle without enjoying contemplation of God's work with him.

38.23.0.en: So it is with every craftsman and master workman who works night as day, and those who engrave the signets of seals, who are diligent in varying the shapes; these set their hearts to reproducing a living image, and watch to finish their craft [27].

38.23.1.en: Society needs those who have gifts in various arts, and it is good that the worker be diligent. However, if these arts are offered by people who walk in the Spirit, they leave beautiful spiritual impressions on many who behold them.

38.23.2.en: The makers of icons used to fast while painting the icon, and took care of their prayers and worship, so that the icon might have its spiritual fruit.

38.23.3.en: And so the smith sitting by the anvil examines closely what he is forging:

38.23.4.en: The flame of the fire melts his flesh, as much as he suffers from the heat of the furnace, he inclines his ear to the sound of the hammer, and his eyes are fixed on the pattern of the vessel.

38.24.0.en: He sets his heart to finish his works, and watches that he may complete their details [28].

38.24.1.en: The smith who suffers from the blaze of the fire and the smoke and the sound of the successive blows on the anvil bears that for the sake of finishing his work. With his faithfulness in work he needs rest and contemplation, which grant him a better life and greater skill in his work.

38.24.2.en: The integration of society is not achieved without craftsmen and their availability, yet setting aside time for study and knowledge to acquire wisdom is necessary in life, for even the trades need wisdom, which God gives to the craftsman, so that his craft comes forth in a form that glorifies God.

38.25.0.en: So also the potter sitting by his work and turning the wheel with his feet, who is always careful about the quality of his work, and also the quantity of his output [29].

38.26.0.en: With his arm he kneads the clay, and with his feet he moves the wheel to curve it. He sets his heart to complete its polishing or glazing, and cleans the furnace with precision and care [30].

38.26.1.en: It befits the potter (or the earthenware maker), who spends his time at his wheel absorbed in making the vessels required of him, then decorating them and painting them and arranging them in the furnace so that they become vessels of various beautiful shapes with wonderful designs, and after that spends the rest of his time cleaning the oven and preparing it for the new batch. It befits the potter, as he prepares the clay to put it on the wheel to shape it, to remember God, the Greatest Potter. And as Origen says of Him:

38.26.2.en: [As long as the earthenware is raw clay it can be reshaped, but once it enters the fire it becomes hard, and if it is broken it cannot be mended. What does this mean? We understand this in a general way first, then, if the Lord permits, we understand it in detail.

38.26.3.en: As long as we are in this life, we are counted as vessels of raw earthenware, either made of vice or of virtue. In any case our vices can be broken so as to become new virtues, just as our progress in virtue is liable to reversal and to falling back. But when we pass the present time and reach the other life, we pass through the fire, whether the fire of the flaming darts of the evil one or the divine fire, since our God is a consuming fire, and whether we are wicked or good, after our breaking (our death) it will not be possible to reshape us and we shall not be capable of being mended. So as long as we are in this life we are as in the hand of the potter: if the vessel falls from his hands he can treat it and mend it. Let us repent of our sins that we have done in the body, and let us return to God with all our hearts now, that He may grant us deliverance and salvation while we have an opportunity for repentance, for after our departure from the world we shall not be able to confess our sins and offer repentance for them[23].]

38.27.0.en: All these trusted in their hands, and each of them is expert in his craft [31].

38.28.0.en: Without them the city is not fit to live in, nor will anyone travel to it or live in it [32].

38.28.1.en: Yet they are not sought in the council of the people, and in the assembly they have no distinction.

38.29.0.en: On the judge's seat they do not sit, and the ordinances of the law they do not understand [33].

38.30.0.en: They cannot give instruction in discipline and judgment, and among those who utter proverbs they are not found; but they keep the fabric of the world firm, and their prayer is in the work of their craft [34].

38.30.1.en: Ben Sira looks at the man who is faithful in his work as one who practises prayer, because he bears the mark of faithfulness that befits the godly believer.

38.31.s.en: I glorify You, O Physician of my soul and my body!

38.31.0.en: v I bless You, O Holy One, for You care for my body as for my spirit!

38.31.1.en: By sin the beauty of my soul vanished, and sickness crept into my body!

38.31.2.en: You did not forsake us; You gave skill and understanding to the sons of men.

38.31.3.en: You offered healing to my body through medicine and physicians.

38.31.4.en: v You brought forth medicines from the earth that You created, and gave skill to man to extract the medicine!

38.31.5.en: You allow me sickness that I may reassess my life, so that I may seek Your righteousness to qualify me to receive a share in Your eternal glories.

38.31.6.en: v By Your resurrection You raised my soul from the death of sin, and prepared for me a place in Your bosom, and granted my body to share with the spirit its glory!

38.31.7.en: In Your love You did not place our hope on earth but in heaven!

38.31.8.en: So if one of mine dies I weep for a time, as You shared the weeping of Mary and Martha for Lazarus, Your beloved!

38.31.9.en: I will not give in to grief lest it destroy my soul.

38.31.10.en: Rather, with the Apostle I will sing: O death, where is thy sting?!

38.31.11.en: I see in the one who has fallen asleep that he has found rest.

38.31.12.en: And I congratulate him on his passing and await with joy my own passing.

38.31.13.en: v O Your wonderful love for all the sons of men.

38.31.14.en: By Your wise ordering You gave men various talents, so that no one may seek to live isolated from his brethren, and no one may be afflicted with smallness of soul because of his trade.

38.31.15.en: All can hear at Your final coming:

38.31.16.en: You were faithful over a few things, I will make you ruler over many things.

38.31.17.en: We shall see great men who were saved as by fire, and from all trades and positions we shall find those who became as the angels of God!

38.31.18.en: The heavenly ones rejoice over all the believers in heaven.

38.31.19.en: They welcome us and glorify the Creator for His salvation of the sons of men!

38.31.20.en: When shall I see all become the Queen-Bride sitting at Your right hand, O King of kings?!
